title: 2017 Teterboro Learjet crash
summary: A Learjet 35A on approach to Teterboro Airport stalled and crashed during a circle-to-land maneuver when the captain allowed an under-qualified first officer to act as pilot flying contrary to company policy. The crew conducted no approach briefing, failed to stabilize the approach, and continued maneuvering below minimum descent altitude with inadequate airspeed. Both pilots were killed in the crash into a commercial building.
probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the pilot-in-command's attempt to salvage an unstabilized visual approach, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall at low altitude. Contributing to the accident were the PIC's decision to allow an unapproved SIC to act as pilot flying, the PIC's inadequate and incomplete preflight planning, and the flight crew's lack of an approach briefing. Also contributing were Trans-Pacific's lack of safety programs to identify poor performance patterns and the FAA's ineffective oversight procedures which failed to identify these company deficiencies (p. 55).

factors.evidence: The first officer (SIC) was rated for single-pilot operations (SIC-0 rated) and was under-qualified as pilot flying; the company's own check airman noted he was 'Not Yet Proficient' with deficiencies in takeoff checks, engine starting, and landing procedures (p. 37, 55).
The captain allowed the unqualified SIC to act as pilot flying in violation of Trans-Pacific's standard operating procedures that restricted SIC-0 pilots to pilot monitoring duties only (p. 37, 55).

No approach briefing was conducted by either crew member, failing to establish situational awareness and clear communication. The crew did not verify the approach procedure or discuss the circle-to-land maneuver (p. 37, 50).

Airspeed decayed during the circle-to-land approach from 127 knots to 111 knots (slowest recorded by radar) while the pilot flying focused on runway alignment rather than monitoring speed indicators. Target airspeed was 139 knots (p. 37-38, 50-51).

The circle-to-land approach was not properly stabilized, with the aircraft descending to the MDA from 1 nm away from runway threshold and continuing inbound rather than beginning the circling maneuver at the final approach fix (TORBY) as directed by ATC (p. 50-51).

The captain focused on coaching the SIC and aligning the aircraft with the runway rather than on cockpit indications showing airspeed decay and descent rate warnings. The captain disregarded EGPWS '500-foot' and 'sink rate, pull up' alerts (p. 37-38, 51).
Aircraft stalled during circle-to-land approach at 35 degree left bank angle with airspeed at 111 knots (versus stall speed of 102 knots). The pilot announced 'stall' in a strained voice (p. 51-52).

After stall, aircraft impacted commercial building at Carlstadt, New Jersey with both pilots killed. Wreckage trail was 315 feet long. Both engines were operating at impact with flaps and landing gear extended (p. 20-21, 34).

events.text: Captain filed instrument flight rules flight plan from Philadelphia to Teterboro; no weather briefing conducted and no approach briefing prepared
Aircraft crosses TORBY (final approach fix) at 1,550 feet altitude; captain did not initiate circle-to-land maneuver at this point as instructed by ATC
First officer acting as pilot flying begins right turn toward runway 1; aircraft at 650 feet altitude and begins descending
EGPWS '500-foot' aural alert sounds; captain disregards alert and tells SIC to disregard it. Aircraft continues descent and right turn
EGPWS 'sink rate, pull up' alert sounds. Aircraft at 350 feet altitude in 28-degree right bank. No go-around initiated
Captain takes control from SIC, stating 'my controls'; instructs SIC to monitor airspeed. Aircraft makes rapid left turn toward runway 1
Captain announces 'stall' in strained voice at 35-degree left bank; SIC responds 'yup'
Aircraft right wing tip impacts roof of office building at Carlstadt, New Jersey; aircraft fragments and catches fire; both pilots killed in impact

cvr.speaker: CAPT
cvr.text: follow the glideslope. do not go below fifteen

recommendations.text: Require all Title 14 CFR Part 135 operators to establish programs for flight crewmembers who have demonstrated performance deficiencies or experienced failures during training and administer additional oversight and training to address and correct performance deficiencies
Develop guidance for Title 14 CFR Part 135 operators to help them create and implement effective crew resource management training programs

Review operators' Learjet 35A operations manuals to determine whether they contain manufacturer-recommended approach speed wind additives and encourage those operators without that information to add it to their operations documents

Issue an advisory circular with guidance on leadership training for upgrading captains at 14 CFR Part 121, 135, and 91K operators, including methods and techniques for effective leadership and professional standards
Require all 14 CFR Part 121, 135, and 91K operators to provide a specific course on leadership training to their upgrading captains
Require all 14 CFR Part 135 operators to install flight data recording devices capable of supporting a flight data monitoring program
After the action in Safety Recommendation A-16-34 is completed, require all 14 CFR Part 135 operators to establish a structured flight data monitoring program that reviews all available data sources
Require all 14 CFR Part 135 operators to establish safety management system programs
Review the Safety Assurance System and develop and implement procedures needed to identify 14 CFR Part 135 operators that do not comply with standard operating procedures
